solution:
**(D)**

Here \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = 2I\), where \(I = I_{3}\).

A scalar matrix commutes with everything, so its powers are found by raising the scalar:
\(A^{6} = (2I)^{6} = 2^{6}I^{6} = 64\,I\)  (since \(I^{6} = I\)).

The options are written in terms of \(A\), so replace \(I\). From \(A = 2I\) we get \(I = \dfrac{1}{2}A\).

\(\therefore A^{6} = 64\,I = 64 \times \dfrac{1}{2}A = 32A\).

Check: \(32A = 32 \times \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 64 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 64 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 64 \end{bmatrix} = 64I\), which agrees with \(A^{6}\).

\(\therefore A^{6} = 32A\).

stem: The inverse of the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} - 1 & 5 \\ - 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) is
solution:
**(A)**

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 5 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(|A| = (-1)(2) - (5)(-3) = -2 + 15 = 13 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.

Co-factors: \(A_{11} = +(2) = 2\), \(A_{12} = -(-3) = 3\), \(A_{21} = -(5) = -5\), \(A_{22} = +(-1) = -1\).

\(\therefore [A_{ij}] = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -5 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\text{adj}(A) = [A_{ij}]^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(\therefore A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\,\text{adj}(A) = \dfrac{1}{13}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\).

Check: \(\dfrac{1}{13}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 5 \\ -3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{13}\begin{bmatrix} -2+15 & 5-5 \\ -6+6 & 15-2 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{13}\begin{bmatrix} 13 & 0 \\ 0 & 13 \end{bmatrix} = I\).

stem: Find the inverse of the matrix \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & - 2 \\ - 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & - 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) using **elementary row transformations**.

If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} x & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & z \end{bmatrix}\) is a non singular matrix, then find \(A^{- 1}\) by **elementary row transformations**. Hence write the inverse of \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & - 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
solution:
Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} x & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & z \end{bmatrix}\).

\(|A| = xyz\), and \(A\) is given non-singular, so \(xyz \neq 0\), i.e. \(x \neq 0\), \(y \neq 0\), \(z \neq 0\).

Write \(A = IA\):
\(\begin{bmatrix} x & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A\).

Apply \(R_{1} \to \dfrac{1}{x}R_{1}\), \(R_{2} \to \dfrac{1}{y}R_{2}\), \(R_{3} \to \dfrac{1}{z}R_{3}\) (legitimate because \(x, y, z\) are all non-zero):

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{x} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{1}{y} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{z} \end{bmatrix} A\).

\(\therefore A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{x} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{1}{y} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{z} \end{bmatrix}\).

**Hence** for \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\) put \(x = 2\), \(y = 1\), \(z = -1\):

\(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\).

Check: \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

stem: **Check whether the matrix** \(\begin{bmatrix} cos\theta & sin\theta \\ - sin\theta & cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\) **is invertible or not**.
solution:
Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\).

A square matrix is invertible if and only if it is non-singular, i.e. \(|A| \neq 0\). So compute \(|A|\):

\(|A| = (\cos\theta)(\cos\theta) - (\sin\theta)(-\sin\theta) = \cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta = 1\).

\(\therefore |A| = 1 \neq 0\) for every value of \(\theta\).

\(\therefore A\) is non-singular, hence \(A\) **is invertible** (for every \(\theta\)).

(In fact \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\,\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\), which is \(A^{T}\).)

stem: Find the **inverse** of \(\begin{bmatrix} cos\theta & - sin\theta & 0 \\ sin\theta & cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) by **elementary row transformations**.
solution:
Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

Expanding along the third row, \(|A| = 1 \cdot (\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta) = 1 \neq 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists.

Write \(A = IA\):
\(\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A\).

Apply the pair of row transformations \(R_{1} \to \cos\theta\,R_{1} + \sin\theta\,R_{2}\) and \(R_{2} \to -\sin\theta\,R_{1} + \cos\theta\,R_{2}\) **simultaneously** (both refer to the original \(R_{1}, R_{2}\); this is a legitimate composition of elementary row operations because the coefficient matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\) has determinant \(1\)).

New \(R_{1}\) on the left: \((\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta,\ -\cos\theta\sin\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta,\ 0) = (1, 0, 0)\).
New \(R_{2}\) on the left: \((-\sin\theta\cos\theta + \cos\theta\sin\theta,\ \sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta,\ 0) = (0, 1, 0)\).

On the right the same combinations of \((1,0,0)\) and \((0,1,0)\) give \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0)\) and \((-\sin\theta, \cos\theta, 0)\). Hence

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} A\).

\(\therefore A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)  (which is \(A^{T}\)).

Check: \(A\,A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta & \cos\theta\sin\theta - \sin\theta\cos\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta\cos\theta - \cos\theta\sin\theta & \sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

stem: Find the matrix of **co-factors** for the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 4 & - 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
solution:
Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 4 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(a_{11} = 1\), \(a_{12} = 3\), \(a_{21} = 4\), \(a_{22} = -1\).

For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix the minor \(M_{ij}\) of an element is the remaining element, and the co-factor is \(A_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}\):

\(A_{11} = (-1)^{1+1}(-1) = -1\)
\(A_{12} = (-1)^{1+2}(4) = -4\)
\(A_{21} = (-1)^{2+1}(3) = -3\)
\(A_{22} = (-1)^{2+2}(1) = 1\)

\(\therefore\) the matrix of co-factors is
\([A_{ij}]_{2 \times 2} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -4 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

(Note this is the matrix of co-factors itself, not the adjoint; \(\text{adj}(A)\) would be its transpose \(\begin{bmatrix} -1 & -3 \\ -4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).)

Check by the expansion property: \(a_{11}A_{11} + a_{12}A_{12} = 1(-1) + 3(-4) = -13\), and \(|A| = (1)(-1) - (3)(4) = -13\). They agree.

stem: Find the **cofactors** of the elements of the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} - 1 & 2 \\ - 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).

solution:
Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).

**Step 1 - find \(\text{adj}\,A\).**
\(A_{11} = (-1)^{1+1}(4) = 4\), \(A_{12} = (-1)^{1+2}(3) = -3\), \(A_{21} = (-1)^{2+1}(2) = -2\), \(A_{22} = (-1)^{2+2}(1) = 1\).

\(\therefore \text{adj}\,A = [A_{ij}]^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

**Step 2 - compute \(A(\text{adj}\,A)\).**
\(A(\text{adj}\,A) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4-6 & -2+2 \\ 12-12 & -6+4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)  ...(i)

**Step 3 - compute \((\text{adj}\,A)A\).**
\((\text{adj}\,A)A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4-6 & 8-8 \\ -3+3 & -6+4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)  ...(ii)

**Step 4 - compute \(|A|\,I\).**
\(|A| = (1)(4) - (2)(3) = -2\), so \(|A|\,I = (-2)\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)  ...(iii)

From (i), (ii) and (iii), \(A(\text{adj}\,A) = (\text{adj}\,A)A = |A|\,I\). Hence verified.

Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(a_{11} = 2\), \(a_{12} = -2\), \(a_{21} = 4\), \(a_{22} = 3\).

Co-factors \(A_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}\):
\(A_{11} = (-1)^{1+1}(3) = 3\), \(A_{12} = (-1)^{1+2}(4) = -4\), \(A_{21} = (-1)^{2+1}(-2) = 2\), \(A_{22} = (-1)^{2+2}(2) = 2\).

\(\therefore [A_{ij}]_{2 \times 2} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(\therefore [A_{ij}]^{T}_{2 \times 2} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ -4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(\therefore \text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ -4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).

Check: \(A\,\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ -4 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6+8 & 4-4 \\ 12-12 & 8+6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 14 & 0 \\ 0 & 14 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(|A| = (2)(3) - (-2)(4) = 14\), so \(A\,\text{adj}(A) = |A|\,I\) as it must be.

subtopic: Solution of Linear Equations using Matrices
stem: Solve the following equations by the method of **reduction**: \(x + 3y + 3z = 12\), \(x + 4y + 4z = 15\), \(x + 3y + 4z = 13\).
solution:
The equations \(x + 3y + 3z = 12\), \(x + 4y + 4z = 15\), \(x + 3y + 4z = 13\) can be written in the form \(AX = B\):

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 12 \\ 15 \\ 13 \end{bmatrix}\).

Apply \(R_{2} \to R_{2} - R_{1}\) and \(R_{3} \to R_{3} - R_{1}\):

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 12 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

Apply \(R_{1} \to R_{1} - 3R_{2}\) and \(R_{2} \to R_{2} - R_{3}\):

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

By equality of matrices, \(x = 3\), \(y = 2\), \(z = 1\).

Check in all three original equations: \(3 + 3(2) + 3(1) = 12\); \(3 + 4(2) + 4(1) = 15\); \(3 + 3(2) + 4(1) = 13\). All three hold.

stem: Solve the following system of equations by the method of **reduction**: \(x + y + z = 6\), \(y + 3z = 11\), \(x + z = 2y\).
solution:
First put the third equation in standard form: \(x + z = 2y\) gives \(x - 2y + z = 0\).

So the system is \(x + y + z = 6\), \(y + 3z = 11\), \(x - 2y + z = 0\), i.e. \(AX = B\):

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 11 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\).

Apply \(R_{3} \to R_{3} - R_{1}\):

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 11 \\ -6 \end{bmatrix}\).

Apply \(R_{3} \to R_{3} + 3R_{2}\):

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 11 \\ 27 \end{bmatrix}\).

The coefficient matrix is now upper triangular, so read the equations off and back-substitute:

\(9z = 27\), so \(z = 3\);
\(y + 3z = 11\), so \(y + 9 = 11\), giving \(y = 2\);
\(x + y + z = 6\), so \(x + 2 + 3 = 6\), giving \(x = 1\).

\(\therefore x = 1\), \(y = 2\), \(z = 3\).

Check in all three original equations: \(1 + 2 + 3 = 6\); \(2 + 3(3) = 11\); and \(x + z = 1 + 3 = 4 = 2(2) = 2y\). All three hold.
